name: Koshari
subtitle: A layered dish of rice, lentils, pasta and chickpeas under tomato sauce and fried onions, sold on Egyptian streets and cooked at home.

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: rice, lentils, chickpeas and pasta, cooked separately

facts.label: Toppings
facts.value: spiced tomato sauce, fried onions, a hot sauce (shatta) and garlic vinegar (da'ah)

parts.text: Koshari is a dish of rice, lentils, chickpeas and pasta, all cooked separately without spices, topped with a peppery hot sauce called shatta, a garlicky vinegar called da'ah, and fried onions.
An Egyptian cook describes it as vegan and easy to make for a large family.
A home cook says her tip for a great koshari is to fry the sliced onions first, so that you get a flavoured oil. She makes it most weekends for her children.
An Egyptian news site calls it often considered Egypt's national dish.
Street vendors traditionally prepare it, though it can be made at home. Diners who are not full can ask for a "kemala", extra spoonfuls.
It is also cooked at family gatherings, a home cook says, as "a dish made with love".

sections.title: Where it comes from: three accounts

parts.text: One account says the dish came from India, where a similar one is called khichri or khichdi, with Indians who accompanied British soldiers to Egypt in the early 1900s, after the First World War; Italian residents are said to have added the pasta.
A home cook gives another date: British colonialism in 1882, when Indians and Italians were based in Egypt, and Egyptians then added the fried onions and the tomato sauce.

A newspaper puts the Indian link in the 1800s, with Italian workers on the Suez Canal arriving by the mid-1800s, and adds that some historians see koshari as developing from the Egyptian mujaddara, a dish of rice, lentils and crisp caramelised onions.
These accounts differ on the date and on who brought what, and this card does not choose between them.

gaps: The origin. The three press articles read give three different dates, from the 1800s to the early 1900s, and none is a historian's study; an Egyptian food historian is needed.
What Egyptians call koshari at home, which varies from family to family. One cook is quoted, and the others are written for readers abroad.
Where and when koshari first appeared in Egyptian cookbooks or shops. Nothing read dates its first sale.
Prices, where to eat it and which places are best known: none of the sources gives them.
The photograph shows a bowl with sauces on the side; where it was taken is not given on its page.
